candidates.name: Sacrococcygeal Teratoma
support_spans: a 34×28 mm sacrococcygeal mass with internal and external components
a 60×70×57 mm sacrococcygeal mass with mixed features—predominantly solid with a 40 mm cyst—and no invasion or compression of pelvic structures or the coccyx (Altman type II)
a 14×7×4 cm, approximately 750 g, reddish sacrococcygeal mass with visible active bleeding
candidates.why: The presence of a sacrococcygeal mass with mixed solid and cystic components, as well as its rapid growth and presence of active bleeding, are characteristic of sacrococcygeal teratoma.

candidates.name: Tumor-related Hemorrhagic Shock

candidates.why: The visible active bleeding from the sacrococcygeal mass and the severe metabolic acidosis suggest tumor-related hemorrhagic shock.

candidates.name: Respiratory Distress Syndrome
support_spans: required positive-pressure ventilation with FiO₂ up to 1.0
ventilated on SIMV with volume guarantee (PIP 25 cm H₂O, PEEP 5 cm H₂O, rate 70/min, FiO₂ 1.0, VG 6 mL/kg)
candidates.why: The need for positive-pressure ventilation and high FiO₂ levels suggests respiratory distress syndrome.

selector.rationale: The presence of a sacrococcygeal mass with mixed features and rapid growth, along with visible active bleeding, supports Sacrococcygeal Teratoma as the primary diagnosis, while Tumor-related Hemorrhagic Shock is a secondary complication.

rejected.label: Neonatal Hypovolemic Shock
rejected.why: Although the patient shows signs of hypovolemic shock, it is more likely a consequence of the sacrococcygeal teratoma and its associated bleeding rather than the primary diagnosis.

rejected.label: Respiratory Distress Syndrome
rejected.why: While the patient required ventilation, the primary issue is the sacrococcygeal teratoma and its complications, making Respiratory Distress Syndrome a secondary concern.
